steps.title: Ensure immediate safety and medical care
steps.detail: Get the employee first aid or emergency medical attention right away. This always comes before any paperwork.

steps.title: Employee reports the injury to their supervisor
steps.detail: The employee (or a coworker on their behalf) should notify their manager/supervisor as soon as possible, even if the injury seems minor.

steps.title: Employer files the official injury report
steps.detail: Submit the employer's incident/injury report to the workers' compensation board for this jurisdiction within the required deadline (varies by province — commonly 3-5 business days; some provinces are stricter, e.g. Nova Scotia ~2 days). Use the form link below.

deadline_notes.Ontario: WSIB requires the employer's report within 3 days of learning of the injury.
deadline_notes.Manitoba: WCB Manitoba requires reporting within 5 business days.
deadline_notes.New Brunswick: WorkSafeNB requires the Employer Report within 3 days.
deadline_notes.Nova Scotia: WCB Nova Scotia recommends reporting within 2 days.
deadline_notes.Newfoundland and Labrador: WorkplaceNL requires the employer's Form 7 within 3 days.
deadline_notes.Quebec: CNESST should be notified promptly; the worker has up to 6 months to file a claim.

steps.title: Support the employee's own claim
steps.detail: The employee typically also needs to file their own worker's report/claim with the board. Point them to the same portal and help them understand the process.

steps.title: Notify internal stakeholders
steps.detail: Loop in your Health & Safety committee/representative and, if the injury is serious, confirm whether a workplace investigation or Ministry notification is separately required.

steps.title: Plan the return-to-work
steps.detail: Once the board/medical provider clears the employee, coordinate a return-to-work plan, including any modified duties or accommodation needs.

steps.title: Confirm jurisdiction and calculate entitlements
steps.detail: Use the Severance Calculator tab to get the statutory minimum notice/severance for this employee's province/territory and years of service.

steps.title: Check for mass/group termination triggers
steps.detail: If this is part of a larger workforce reduction, use the Reorg Scenario Planner tab — it flags when headcount crosses a jurisdiction's mass-termination threshold, which usually adds extended notice and a filing requirement with the labour ministry.

steps.title: Check for company policy or contractual entitlements
steps.detail: Compare the statutory minimum against any employment contract or company severance policy — the employee is entitled to whichever is greater. The Severance Calculator can reconcile this for you if you paste/upload the policy.

steps.title: Prepare the termination letter and final pay
steps.detail: Include the reason (if disclosed), effective date, and a breakdown of notice/pay in lieu, severance, accrued vacation pay, and any other amounts owed.

steps.title: Issue the Record of Employment (ROE)
steps.detail: Federally required for every employee who has an interruption of earnings, regardless of province. Use ROE Web to submit it.

steps.title: Retain records
steps.detail: Keep the calculation, termination letter, and ROE on file — this is also what the app's audit trail captures automatically if you used the calculator.

steps.title: Confirm the leave type and eligibility
steps.detail: Identify which statutory leave applies (sick, parental, family/caregiver, bereavement, domestic violence leave, etc.) and confirm the employee meets the jurisdiction's eligibility criteria (e.g. minimum service length).

steps.title: Document the request
steps.detail: Get the request in writing with the expected start date and duration. Some leave types require advance notice from the employee; others don't.

steps.title: Coordinate wage-replacement benefits
steps.detail: Determine whether Employment Insurance (EI) special benefits or the company's short/long-term disability plan applies, and point the employee to the right application.

steps.title: Confirm job protection obligations
steps.detail: Most statutory leaves come with job/position protection — confirm what role the employee returns to and any benefits continuation requirements during the leave.

steps.title: Plan the return-to-work
steps.detail: Check in ahead of the expected return date and confirm any accommodation needs before the employee is back.

steps.title: Document the concern
steps.detail: Record what was reported, when, by whom, and any immediate steps taken (e.g. separating the parties involved).

steps.title: Assess duty to accommodate
steps.detail: If the concern relates to disability, family status, religion, or another protected ground, determine whether accommodation is required up to the point of undue hardship.

steps.title: Conduct or commission an investigation
steps.detail: Depending on severity, this may be internal (HR-led) or require an external investigator. Keep the process confidential and document findings.

steps.title: Implement remedies
steps.detail: Based on findings, this could include policy changes, disciplinary action, training, or accommodation measures.

steps.title: Know the external escalation path
steps.detail: If the employee isn't satisfied with the internal resolution, they may file with the applicable human rights tribunal/commission. Use the link below to know where that is for this jurisdiction.
